etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English sor, from Old English sār (“ache, wound”, noun) and sār (“painful, grievous”, adjective), from Proto-West Germanic *sair, from Proto-Germanic *sairaz (adjective) from Proto-Indo-European *sh₂eyro-, enlargement of *sh₂ey- (“to be fierce, afflict”).

See also Dutch zeer (“sore, ache”), Danish sår (“wound”), German sehr (“very”); also Hittite [script needed] (sāwar, “anger”), Welsh hoed (“pain”), Ancient Greek αἱμωδία (haimōdía, “sensation of having teeth on edge”).

definitions.definition: Causing pain or discomfort; painfully sensitive.
Sensitive; tender; easily pained, grieved, or vexed; very susceptible of irritation.

quote.text: Malice and hatred are very fretting and vexatious, and apt to make our minds sore and uneasy.

definitions.definition: (informal) Feeling animosity towards someone; annoyed or angered.

quote.citation: 1951, J. D. Salinger, The Catcher in the Rye, Boston, Mass.: Little, Brown and Company, →OCLC, page 53:
quote.text: “God damn it.” He was sore as hell. He was really furious.

quote.citation: 2024 May 1, “Network News: Do TfN and the DfT actually respect each other?”, in RAIL, number 1008, page 13:
quote.text: TfN is clearly very sore about last year's axing of part of HS2.

quote.citation: c. 1599–1602 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Hamlet, Prince of Denmarke”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene i]:
quote.text: […] and your water is a sore decayer of your whoreson dead body.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Joshua 9:24:
quote.text: And they answered Ioshua, and said, Because it was certainely told thy seruants, how that the Lord thy God commanded his seruant Moses to giue you all the land, and to destroy all the inhabitants of the land from before you, therefore we were sore afraid of our liues because of you, and haue done this thing.

quote.citation: 1859, Alfred Tennyson, “Elaine”, in Idylls of the King, London: Edward Moxon & Co., […], →OCLC, pages 174–175:
quote.text: But on that day when Lancelot fled the lists, / His party, knights of utmost North and West, / Lords of waste marches, kings of desolate isles, / Came round their great Pendragon, saying to him / 'Lo, Sire, our knight thro' whom we won the day / Hath gone sore wounded, and hath left his prize / Untaken, crying that his prize is death.'

quote.citation: 1879, R[ichard] J[efferies], “The Old Punt: A Curious ‘Turnpike’”, in The Amateur Poacher, London: Smith, Elder, & Co., […], →OCLC, pages 19–20:
quote.text: Orion hit a rabbit once; but though sore wounded it got to the bury, and, struggling in, the arrow caught the side of the hole and was drawn out.

quote.citation: 1885, Richard F. Burton, The Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night:
quote.text: And indeed I blamed myself and sore repented me of having taken compassion on him and continued in this condition, suffering fatigue not to be described,  […]

quote.citation: 1919, Edgar Rice Burroughs, Jungle Tales of Tarzan‎[2]:
quote.text: [… they] were often sore pressed to follow the trail at all, and at best were so delayed that in the afternoon of the second day, they still had not overhauled the fugitive.

definitions.definition: An injured, infected, inflamed or diseased patch of skin.

quote.citation: 1822, [Walter Scott], Peveril of the Peak. […], volume (please specify |volume=I to IV), Edinburgh:  […]  Archibald Constable and Co.; London: Hurst, Robinson, and Co., →OCLC:
quote.text: I see plainly where his sore lies.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To mutilate the legs or feet of (a horse) in order to induce a particular gait.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English sor (“sorrel”), from Old French sor (“sorrel; reddish”). Compare French saur (“(archaic) reddish-brown; describing a young bird of prey”).

definitions.definition: A young hawk or falcon in its first year.

quote.citation: 1596, Edmund Spenser, An Hymne of Heavenly Beautie:
quote.text: Of the soare faulcon so I learn to fly

definitions.definition: A young buck in its fourth year.

quote.citation: c. 1595–1596 (date written), William Shakespeare, “Loues Labour’s Lost”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene ii]:
quote.text: Some say a Sore, but not a sore, till now made sore with shooting.The Dogges did yell, put ell to Sore, then Sorell iumps from thicket:Or Pricket-sore, or else Sorell, the people fall a hooting.If Sore be sore, then ell to Sore, makes fiftie sores O sorell:Of one sore I an hundred make by adding but one more L.
